name: Broadway Triangle
headline: New housing filling in slowly
why: Former Pfizer factory land in Williamsburg that sat empty for decades while neighbors fought over who new housing would serve. Rabsky Group is now building about 1,150 apartments here.
history: Pfizer opened here in 1849 and by the early 1900s occupied the full block now called Broadway Triangle. Manufacturing ran until 2008, after its HQ moved to Manhattan in 1961. Earlier use is unknown.
now: Rabsky's buildings keep opening in phases, with a quarter of the apartments set aside as affordable. A lottery for 120 of those affordable apartments at 11 Gerry St closed in March 2026.
owner: Rabsky Group owns most of the land. Some nearby lots still belong to the city.

name: Greenpoint Hospital Campus
headline: Affordable homes rising, seniors wait
neighborhood: 288 Jackson St · Bed-Stuy / East Williamsburg border
why: The old Greenpoint Hospital, closed since 1982, is being turned into about 557 affordable homes, including senior housing, plus a 200-bed homeless shelter, built in four stages.
history: Before the hospital, this was Peter Cooper's glue factory (c. 1845-1915), one of the city's largest. The hospital opened October 4, 1915, run by the city, and closed in December 1982 after 70 years.
now: The shelter opened in 2025 and a 311-apartment building is nearly done, with its housing lottery due soon. But the city moved a temporary shelter onto the site in March 2026, stalling the senior housing. Neighbors rallied Sept 17.
owner: The city owns the site. Hudson Companies and St. Nicks Alliance are building the housing; the nonprofit Project Renewal runs the shelter.

name: Monitor Point
headline: Three towers approved
neighborhood: 40-56 Quay St · Greenpoint waterfront, by Bushwick Inlet Park
why: A plan to replace an old MTA repair yard and an empty museum lot next to Bushwick Inlet with three apartment towers. Many neighbors wanted this land added to the park the city promised in 2005.
history: 56 Quay St was Motiva land, donated in 2003 to found the Greenpoint Monitor Museum, honoring the nearby shipyard that built the ironclad USS Monitor in 1862. 40 Quay St was an MTA auto-repair yard.
now: The City Council approved it July 16, 2026, after Council Member Lincoln Restler pushed the developer to make half of the roughly 1,300 apartments affordable. The towers will be 56, 41 and 35 stories tall.
owner: The MTA owns the land and will lease it to developer Gotham Organization for 99 years.

name: Fulton-Howard West
headline: Proposed affordable housing
neighborhood: Bed-Stuy Multi-Service Center, 1958 Fulton St · Bedford-Stuyvesant (city-owned site)
why: An aging city-owned social services building in Bed-Stuy, plus empty lots beside it, that the city wants to replace with all-affordable housing and new space for the services now inside.
history: The 5-story building was built in sections from 1912-1925 and first housed P.S. 28, a public school that did not fully vacate until 2019. No source documents earlier use of the lot.
now: In May 2026 Mayor Mamdani's administration started asking neighbors what they want here. Their input through the summer will shape the city's search for a developer to build hundreds of affordable homes.

name: River Ring
headline: Tax break secured, towers years off
neighborhood: River St between N 1st and N 3rd Sts · Williamsburg waterfront
why: Parking lots on the Williamsburg waterfront, once a Con Edison fuel depot, where developer Two Trees plans two tall apartment towers, a YMCA, a public beach and a waterfront park.
history: This was Con Edison's North First St fuel-oil terminal. Two Trees bought it in 2019 for $150M and removed the tanks, though old foundations and seawall pieces remain. Earlier use is unconfirmed.
now: In May 2026 the state gave Two Trees extra time to keep a large property-tax break it says the project needs. About 1,200 apartments are planned, 30% affordable, but the first tower likely won't be finished until 2033.

name: Greenpoint Landing, Phase Two
headline: Three towers planned
neighborhood: 21 & 37 Freeman St, 209 West St · Greenpoint waterfront, north of Transmitter Park
why: Proposal to fill vacant land along the Greenpoint waterfront with about 1,000 homes across 3 apartment buildings, along with a public park. This is a new piece of the 'Greenpoint Landing' master plan to add 5,500 homes to the waterfront.
history: This stretch of waterfront held some of the 50+ oil refineries that operated 1860s-1960s. WNYC's transmitter ran just south of here 1937-1990. No source names an earlier occupant of this site.
now: The developers, Domain, LMXD and Park Tower Group, plan buildings of 40, 30 and 9 stories, with 300 affordable apartments. They lined up $114 million in loans for the land in Aug 2025 and aimed to start building in summer 2026.
owner: Park Tower Group, which leads the larger Greenpoint Landing plan, with The Domain Companies and LMXD.

name: Transmitter Park
headline: Marina plan scrapped
why: A small city park on the Greenpoint waterfront, opened in 2012 where WNYC's radio transmitter stood. A plan to add a restaurant and a 40-boat marina here met strong neighborhood pushback.
history: This spot was Greenpoint's ferry terminal 1853-1933. The city set it aside for WNYC radio in 1935. The New Deal-funded transmitter building opened in 1937 and broadcast until 1990.
now: The Parks Department dropped the restaurant and marina plan on Sept 15, 2026, after local objections. Next it will look for an operator for a public restroom, and may drop the rule to restore the 1937 radio building in favor of a plaque.

name: Bushwick Inlet Park
headline: Promised park still unfinished
why: A waterfront park the city promised in 2005 in exchange for letting developers build taller along the Williamsburg and Greenpoint shore. More than 20 years later, most of it still isn't built.
history: The largest undelivered section sits on the former Astral Oil Works (later Standard Oil, sold in the 1940s), then the Bayside Fuel Oil Depot until it closed in 2010. Tanks came down in 2019.
now: A new section around the inlet opened April 30, 2026, bringing the park to about 9 of its promised 28 acres. The next piece, the old CitiStorage site, is waiting on a slow toxic cleanup, and finishing the park is $75 to $100 million short.
owner: The Parks Department owns the land.

name: Grand Army Plaza Redesign
headline: Plaza redesign proposed
why: The busy traffic circle at the entrance to Prospect Park, around the landmark arch, which the city wants to make safer and friendlier for people walking and biking.
history: Laid out as Olmsted and Vaux's Prospect Park entrance starting in 1866. The Soldiers' and Sailors' Arch went up 1889-92. The current Bailey Fountain dates to 1929-32. Landmarked 1973-75.
now: In April 2026 the city proposed closing a road to connect the arch directly to Prospect Park, adding about 42% more public space. The plan still needs detailed design and landmarks approval before any construction.
owner: The city; the Department of Transportation runs the streets.

name: Park Avenue / BQE Corridor
headline: Ideas for space under the BQE
neighborhood: 100 Park Ave (representative point) · under the BQE, Fort Greene/Clinton Hill end of the corridor
why: The stretch of Park Ave in Brooklyn under the elevated BQE highway, near the Navy Yard, where the city is looking at how to make the dark, underused space below safer and more useful.
history: Before the BQE, this was an at-grade industrial street near the Navy Yard (Rockwood Chocolate, Drake's Cakes). This segment was among the last finished, completed around 1960.
now: In October 2024 the city's transportation department floated long-term ideas for the BQE, including this stretch: safer crossings, bike and bus lanes, new plazas, and covering parts of the highway.
owner: New York State DOT; the state owns the highway.
